steps.conclusion: Lesson-size problems recur across chapters despite the stated 2–5-minute durations. Examples include all four decimal operations in four minutes; multiples, divisibility, primes and factorization in four minutes; both substitution and elimination methods in five minutes; and amplitude, variance and standard deviation in five minutes. These bundles are too ambitious for learners starting from zero. Equivalent compound-interest rates, quadratic equations and calculation of standard deviation also extend beyond the specified beginner foundations without adequate scaffolding.

Some prerequisites arrive late: scale-based measurement conversions precede the units chapter, and classifying numbers using the square root of two precedes the introduction of roots. Annual-to-monthly compound-rate conversion requires general roots or an explicitly taught tool workflow, whereas the earlier roots lesson covers square and cube roots. Some lesson outcomes also underspecify their descriptions: the roots lesson includes cube roots but its can-do and skills cover only square roots.

Make mathematical conditions explicit in the relevant lesson descriptions: direct and inverse proportionality require a constant ratio or product, not merely quantities changing together or in opposite directions; counting favorable outcomes over possible outcomes assumes equally likely elementary outcomes. These clarifications would strengthen the outline's otherwise substantial emphasis on interpretation and checking.
